Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- Rapes targeting girls as young as seven are on the increase in Afghanistan where conditions for women are little better than under the Taliban, the U.N. and rights groups say. Conditions for women are little better than they were under the hardline Taliban regime, the U.N. says. In its annual report on human rights, the U.N. warned conditions were deteriorating in the war-ravaged country despite U.S.-led efforts after the 2001 removal from power of the hardline militia. "Violence is tolerated or condoned within the family and community, within traditional and religious leadership circles, as well as the formal and informal justice system," said Navi Pillay, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights. The "Afghan government has failed to adequately protect the rights of women despite constitutional guarantees." With a resurgent Taliban targeting NATO forces, government security forces and civilians, violence has been on the increase in Afghanistan.. The number of civilian casualties in 2008 totaled 2,118 -- the highest number recorded since the ouster of the Taliban in 2001, the U.N. said, urging greater protecting for ordinary Afghans. Violence against women comes in the form of rape, "honor killings," early and forced marriages, sexual abuse and slavery, the report says. "The security is the big issue," said Suraya Pakzad, founder of the Voice of Women Organization, which promotes education and awareness of women's rights and protects women and girls at risk in Afghanistan. "Because of security we, unfortunately, day by day, we have to pull out of areas where last year we operated, we have our operations. We were able to work with the women, but this year we cannot," she said. "We have to leave the area because security is getting worse day by day." "Rapes in the country have been growing tremendously, particularly child rapes within the ages of 9, 8, 7, even lesser than that," said Wazhma Frogh, director of Global Rights Afghanistan. "So these are the issues that are all born by this lack of security where women have no place in ... security decisions." Domestic violence against child brides is widespread, said Suraya Pakzad, the founder of the Voice of Women organization, who was married at age 14 and has six children. She said girls as young as 10 face "violation" by husbands 40 years their senior. "By the end ... women, or girls, run away." But women without husbands, especially widows, may have it even worse in Afghanistan, the report says. Without a spouse, the women are reduced to begging to feed their children. Options outside the home are limited where the Taliban holds sway in Afghanistan. The Taliban's interpretation of strict Islamic law, or sharia, has included banning girls from school and the workplace. Even in areas not overrun by the Taliban, women face risks outside the home. "The assassination of the most prominent national female senior police officer, in Kandahar in September 2008, underscores the tremendous risks faced by women in public life," the report says.

outputs.L2:
UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — The United Nations and human rights organizations say sexual assaults against girls, including children as young as seven, are rising in Afghanistan, where women’s lives have improved only slightly compared with the period of Taliban rule.

In its yearly human rights assessment, the U.N. said the situation in Afghanistan was worsening, despite U.S.-led efforts following the removal of the Taliban from power in 2001. Navi Pillay, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, said abuse is accepted or excused in families, communities, traditional and religious leadership structures, and both official and unofficial justice systems. She added that the Afghan government has not done enough to defend women’s rights, even though those rights are protected in the constitution.

As the Taliban has regained strength and attacked NATO troops, Afghan security forces, and civilians, violence across the country has increased. According to the U.N., 2,118 civilians were killed in 2008, the largest annual total recorded since the Taliban was ousted in 2001. The organization called for stronger protection for Afghan civilians.

The report says women face many forms of violence, including rape, so-called “honor killings,” forced and underage marriage, sexual exploitation, and slavery.

Suraya Pakzad, who founded the Voice of Women Organization, said worsening security is a major obstacle. Her group works in Afghanistan to educate people about women’s rights and to protect vulnerable women and girls. Pakzad said that, because of the deteriorating security situation, the organization has had to withdraw from places where it had been active the previous year. She said they had previously been able to work with women in those areas, but could no longer remain there safely.

Wazhma Frogh, director of Global Rights Afghanistan, said rapes have increased sharply, especially assaults on children aged nine, eight, seven, and even younger. She linked the problem to the lack of security and the exclusion of women from decisions about security.

Pakzad also said domestic abuse against girls forced into marriage is common. Pakzad herself married at 14 and has six children. She said girls as young as 10 can be subjected to abuse by husbands who may be 40 years older than they are. In many cases, she said, women or girls eventually flee.

The report also says that women without husbands, particularly widows, may face even harsher conditions in Afghanistan. Many are left with no choice but to beg in order to provide food for their children.

In parts of Afghanistan controlled by the Taliban, women have few opportunities outside the home. The Taliban’s strict interpretation of Islamic law, or sharia, has included barring girls from education and preventing women from working.

Even in areas not under Taliban control, women who take public roles remain in danger. The report cited the September 2008 assassination in Kandahar of the country’s most prominent senior female police officer as an example of the serious threats faced by women in public life.
outputs.L3:
The United Nations and international rights organizations have reported a worsening situation for women and girls in Afghanistan, warning that violence against them is increasing across the country. Reports include severe abuses such as rape, with victims said to include children as young as seven. These cases have raised serious concern among human rights advocates, who say Afghan women and girls remain highly vulnerable to violence, intimidation, and abuse.

According to the U.N., the conditions faced by Afghan women are still only marginally better than they were under Taliban rule, despite the adoption of constitutional protections and years of international engagement since 2001. Although legal reforms and aid programs were intended to improve women’s rights, the U.N. says many women continue to face discrimination, forced marriage, domestic violence, and limited access to justice.

Navi Pillay, the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, said violence against women in Afghanistan is often tolerated or ignored within families, communities, religious leadership, and the justice system. She criticized the Afghan government for failing to adequately protect women’s rights and for not ensuring that perpetrators of abuse are held accountable. Rights groups have similarly argued that weak enforcement of the law and deeply rooted social attitudes allow violence against women to continue with impunity.

The broader security situation in Afghanistan has also deteriorated. Civilian casualties rose to 2,118 in 2008, the highest number recorded since the fall of the Taliban regime. The increase came amid worsening violence, expanding insurgent activity, and a resurgence of the Taliban in several parts of the country.

Women’s rights advocates say this decline in security has had a direct impact on their work. As violence spreads, organizations that once provided support, protection, education, and legal assistance to women and girls have been forced to withdraw from some areas. This has left many Afghan women with fewer resources and less protection at a time when threats against them are growing.
outputs.L4:
The United Nations and several human rights organizations say violence against women and girls in Afghanistan is worsening, despite legal reforms introduced after the fall of the Taliban in 2001 and constitutional guarantees meant to protect women’s rights.

Reports from U.N. agencies and advocacy groups describe a disturbing rise in abuses including rape, so-called honor killings, forced marriage, domestic violence, and sexual exploitation. Women’s rights activists say many cases are never reported because victims fear retaliation, social stigma, or punishment by their own families and communities. In rural areas especially, traditional power structures and weak law enforcement often leave women with little protection or access to justice.

Although Afghanistan’s post-2001 constitution formally recognized equality before the law and the government adopted measures intended to improve women’s rights, campaigners say those protections have rarely been enforced. Police, prosecutors, and courts have frequently failed to investigate crimes against women, while perpetrators often escape punishment. In some cases, victims themselves have been detained or blamed for the violence committed against them.

The situation has been made worse by the country’s deteriorating security. As insurgent attacks, armed conflict, and lawlessness have spread, women and girls have become increasingly vulnerable. Human rights monitors have pointed to rising reports of rape of children, forced marriages used to settle disputes or debts, and attacks on women who attend school, work outside the home, or take part in public life.

The findings suggest that the Afghan government has failed to provide meaningful protection for women and girls. Activists argue that legal reforms alone are not enough without functioning courts, trained police, shelters, education, and political will to challenge entrenched discrimination.

The reports also come against the backdrop of record civilian casualties, highlighting the broader collapse in security across the country. For many Afghan women, rights groups say, daily life remains marked by fear, intimidation, and violence. Despite the formal gains made since the Taliban were removed from power, conditions for many women and girls remain only marginally better than they were under Taliban rule.
outputs.L5:
The **United Nations** is one of the world’s most important international organizations, bringing countries together to address global challenges such as peace and security, human rights, climate change, poverty, and humanitarian crises. Founded in 1945 after World War II, the United Nations provides a forum where nations can discuss problems, negotiate solutions, and coordinate international action.

Media organizations like **CNN** often report on the work of the United Nations, especially during major global events. Coverage may include speeches at the UN General Assembly, Security Council debates, peacekeeping missions, refugee emergencies, climate summits, and international responses to conflicts or natural disasters. Through news reporting, CNN helps inform the public about decisions made at the United Nations and how those decisions may affect people around the world.

The relationship between global institutions and the media is important because it helps promote awareness and accountability. When the United Nations launches an appeal for humanitarian aid, discusses sanctions, or calls for peace negotiations, news outlets such as CNN can bring those issues to a wider audience. This can influence public opinion, encourage international cooperation, and highlight crises that might otherwise receive limited attention.

In today’s interconnected world, the United Nations and international news media both play significant roles. The United Nations works to support diplomacy and global cooperation, while CNN and other news organizations help explain these efforts to viewers and readers across the globe. Together, they contribute to a better understanding of international affairs and the challenges facing humanity.

counterfactuals.output:
UNITED NATIONS — Conditions for women in Afghanistan remain deeply troubling years after the fall of the Taliban, with worsening insecurity, civilian casualties and entrenched violence undermining gains in education, health care and public participation, U.N. officials and rights advocates said.

A report presented at the United Nations warned that many Afghan women continue to face forced marriages, domestic abuse and so-called honor killings, particularly in rural areas where government authority is weak and armed groups hold sway. The report said fear of violence has restricted women’s movement, kept girls out of school and discouraged women from working in public life.

U.N. officials said the broader security situation has contributed sharply to women’s vulnerability. Civilian casualties rose significantly in 2008 as fighting intensified between Afghan and international forces and insurgent groups. The violence affected families across the country, with women often left as widows, displaced from their homes or forced to support households without protection or income.

Although the fall of the Taliban in 2001 opened space for Afghan women to return to schools, workplaces and politics, the report said progress has been uneven and fragile. In many provinces, traditional practices and intimidation have continued to deny women basic rights.

Human rights monitors cited forced marriage as one of the most persistent abuses, including marriages involving girls and arrangements used to settle disputes between families. Honor killings also remain a serious concern, with perpetrators often escaping punishment because of weak law enforcement, social pressure and limited access to courts.

U.N. representatives urged Afghan authorities and international donors to strengthen protections for women, improve access to justice and ensure that security efforts do not overlook the particular risks faced by women and girls.

“The legal rights of Afghan women mean little if they cannot safely leave their homes, attend school, seek medical care or report violence,” one U.N. official said.

The report called for expanded shelters, more female police officers, better prosecution of gender-based violence and continued support for women’s education. It also warned that without improved security, Afghanistan’s hard-won gains for women could erode further.

## Afghan women’s rights remain in crisis, rights groups say, with freedoms sharply curtailed under Taliban rule

Afghan women and girls continue to face severe restrictions on education, work, movement and public life, with their rights dramatically rolled back since the Taliban returned to power, according to findings from the United Nations and leading human rights organizations.

The Taliban, which seized control of Afghanistan in August 2021, has imposed a growing web of rules that have pushed women and girls out of classrooms, workplaces and much of public society. The measures have drawn condemnation from the U.N., Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and other groups, which say Afghanistan has become one of the most repressive countries in the world for women.

U.N. officials have repeatedly warned that Taliban policies amount to systematic discrimination against women and girls. The restrictions include bans on girls attending secondary school and university, severe limits on women working for non-governmental organizations and the United Nations, and rules requiring women to travel with male guardians in many circumstances.

Human rights groups say the result is a society in which women’s rights are not merely restricted but increasingly erased from public life.

“The Taliban’s policies have made Afghanistan the most serious women’s rights crisis in the world,” Human Rights Watch has said in its reporting on the country. Amnesty International has similarly described the crackdown as part of a broader campaign of repression, affecting women activists, protesters, journalists and professionals.

Women who have protested the restrictions have faced intimidation, detention and abuse, rights groups say. Many demonstrations that emerged after the Taliban takeover were quickly suppressed, and activists have reported being threatened or forced into hiding.

The Taliban has defended its policies as being in line with its interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. Taliban officials have at times claimed that restrictions on girls’ education are temporary, but more than two years after the group’s return to power, most teenage girls remain barred from school.

The consequences have been far-reaching. Aid agencies say the exclusion of women from many jobs has worsened Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis by limiting the delivery of assistance, especially to women and children. Female aid workers have played a critical role in reaching vulnerable communities in a country where cultural norms often prevent male staff from interacting with women beneficiaries.

The U.N. has also warned that the restrictions have harmed Afghanistan’s economy, health system and social fabric. Women doctors, teachers, civil servants and aid workers were once central to public life in many parts of the country. Their exclusion has deepened poverty and reduced access to essential services.

Before the Taliban takeover, Afghan women had made gains over two decades, particularly in urban areas. Millions of girls attended school, women served in parliament, worked as judges, journalists and police officers, and participated in civic life. Those gains were uneven and fragile, especially outside major cities, but rights groups say the Taliban’s return has dismantled much of that progress.

For many Afghan women, the change has been devastating. Former students have described being trapped at home with no clear future. Professional women have lost careers. Activists say the country’s women have been stripped of the basic right to choose their own path.

International pressure has so far produced little change. No country has formally recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s legitimate government, and foreign governments have repeatedly cited women’s rights as a key obstacle to normalization. But the Taliban has continued to tighten restrictions despite diplomatic isolation and widespread condemnation.

U.N. experts have urged the international community not to treat women’s rights as a secondary issue in negotiations with the Taliban. They argue that any engagement with Afghanistan’s rulers must place the rights of women and girls at the center.

Rights groups say the situation is not simply a domestic policy dispute, but a human rights emergency.

As one U.N. assessment put it, Afghan women and girls are being excluded from nearly every aspect of public life — a reality that has left many with freedoms only marginally different from, and in some areas worse than, those they endured during the Taliban’s first period in power in the 1990s.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed wire-service summary of a U.N. report on Afghanistan saying rape of young girls, domestic violence, child marriage, and attacks on women in public life are worsening amid rising Taliban violence.
counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan —** Violence against women and girls in Afghanistan is worsening, with reported cases of rape of young girls, domestic abuse, forced and child marriage, and attacks on women in public life increasing as Taliban-led insecurity spreads, according to a United Nations report.

The report says Afghan women and girls continue to face “pervasive” violence in their homes and communities, while women who work in government, education, policing, the judiciary, media and civil society are increasingly being threatened, intimidated or attacked. The U.N. warned that the deteriorating security situation, particularly in areas with a strong Taliban presence, is eroding the limited gains women have made since the fall of the Taliban government in 2001.

U.N. officials said the violence is both widespread and underreported, with many victims deterred from seeking justice by fear of retaliation, social stigma, family pressure and weak law enforcement. In many cases, the report said, police, prosecutors and courts fail to act, or cases are resolved through informal mediation that often pressures victims to return to abusive homes or accept settlements that do not protect them.

The report highlights particular concern over child marriage and forced marriage, saying girls are frequently married off to settle disputes, repay debts or ease poverty. It also cites cases of sexual violence against children and says perpetrators are often shielded by powerful local figures or by families unwilling to pursue criminal complaints.

Domestic violence remains one of the most common abuses, the U.N. said, with women reporting beatings, confinement, threats and other mistreatment by husbands or relatives. Although Afghanistan has a law aimed at eliminating violence against women, implementation remains uneven, especially outside major cities.

Women active in public life face additional dangers, the report said. Female officials, police officers, teachers, health workers, journalists and rights advocates have been targeted in threats and attacks, often by insurgents who oppose women’s participation outside the home. The U.N. said such violence has a chilling effect, discouraging women from working, attending school or taking part in political and civic life.

The report links the worsening situation to the broader rise in Taliban violence and the weakness of state institutions in contested areas. As insurgents gain influence, the U.N. said, conservative restrictions on women’s movement, education and employment are being imposed in some communities, sometimes through threats or public punishments.

U.N. officials urged the Afghan government to strengthen enforcement of laws protecting women, prosecute perpetrators, expand shelters and legal aid, and ensure that women in public roles receive adequate protection. The report also called on religious and community leaders to condemn violence against women and on international donors to maintain support for women’s rights programs.

The findings underscore fears among Afghan women’s groups that insecurity and political instability could reverse years of fragile progress. Rights advocates have warned that any peace efforts involving the Taliban must not sacrifice constitutional protections for women or allow abuses to go unpunished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news story about the increase in rapes targeting girls as young as seven in Afghanistan, citing the U.N., Voice of Women Organization, Global Rights Afghanistan, and the impact of worsening security.
counterfactuals.output:
**Reports Warn of Rising Sexual Violence Against Young Girls in Afghanistan Amid Worsening Security**

*KABUL —* Human rights groups and United Nations officials are warning of a disturbing rise in sexual violence against girls in Afghanistan, with advocates reporting cases involving children as young as seven as insecurity, poverty, and weak access to justice deepen across the country.

According to U.N. agencies monitoring conditions for women and children in Afghanistan, the collapse of protective services, restrictions on women’s movement and work, and the country’s deteriorating security environment have left girls increasingly vulnerable to abuse. The U.N. has repeatedly raised concerns that survivors of gender-based violence face major barriers to reporting attacks and obtaining medical, legal, and psychosocial support.

Local women’s rights advocates say the true scale of the crisis is likely far higher than what is publicly documented. The Voice of Women Organization, an Afghan women-led advocacy group, has reported receiving accounts of rape and sexual abuse targeting young girls, including children, in several parts of the country. Activists say many families remain silent because of stigma, fear of retaliation, or lack of trust in authorities.

Global Rights Afghanistan has also warned that worsening security conditions have created an environment in which perpetrators act with growing impunity. The organization says displacement, economic desperation, and the erosion of community protection systems have increased risks for girls, particularly in rural areas and among families already affected by conflict.

“Girls are being exposed to violence at an age when they should be in school and protected by their communities,” one Afghan women’s rights advocate said. “Instead, many families feel they have nowhere safe to turn.”

The reported increase comes as Afghanistan faces overlapping crises: widespread poverty, restrictions on female education and employment, reduced access to health care, and limited shelter services for survivors of abuse. Women’s rights groups say these factors have made it harder for victims to escape unsafe homes, report crimes, or receive trauma care.

Security deterioration has also affected the ability of aid workers and rights monitors to document cases. In some provinces, advocates say threats from armed actors, local powerbrokers, or abusive family members prevent survivors from seeking help. Others fear that reporting sexual violence could lead to social punishment against the victim rather than accountability for the perpetrator.

The U.N. has urged authorities and international donors to strengthen protection systems for women and children, expand confidential survivor services, and ensure that cases of sexual violence are investigated. Rights organizations say that without urgent intervention, more girls will remain trapped in silence.

“Sexual violence against children is one of the gravest violations of human rights,” Global Rights Afghanistan said in its recent warnings. “Ending impunity and restoring protection mechanisms must be treated as an emergency.”

Advocates are calling for safe reporting channels, child-focused medical and psychological care, legal assistance, and expanded support for Afghan women-led organizations working on the front lines. They also warn that continued restrictions on women aid workers and civil society organizations will further weaken the country’s ability to protect children from abuse.

For many survivors, campaigners say, the immediate need is safety — and the chance to be heard without fear.

“The world must not look away,” said a representative of the Voice of Women Organization. “These girls need protection, justice, and long-term support.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
